```{python}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- style
# Figures carry their own light surface so they stay legible whatever
# theme the surrounding site uses.
PAL = dict(
    kaplan="#eb6834", chin="#2a78d6", third="#1baf7a",
    surface="#fcfcfb", ink="#101318", ink2="#4b5159",
    muted="#848b95", rule="#e0e3e8", rule_strong="#c3c9d2",
)

mpl.rcParams.update({
    "figure.facecolor": PAL["surface"], "axes.facecolor": PAL["surface"],
    "savefig.facecolor": PAL["surface"], "savefig.bbox": "tight",
    "font.family": "sans-serif", "font.size": 10.5,
    "text.color": PAL["ink"], "axes.labelcolor": PAL["ink2"],
    "xtick.color": PAL["muted"], "ytick.color": PAL["muted"],
    "axes.edgecolor": PAL["rule_strong"], "axes.linewidth": 0.8,
    "xtick.major.size": 3, "ytick.major.size": 3,
    "xtick.minor.size": 1.8, "ytick.minor.size": 1.8,
    "grid.color": PAL["rule"], "grid.linewidth": 0.8,
    "axes.grid": True, "axes.axisbelow": True,
    "legend.frameon": False, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
})

def style(ax, xlabel=None, ylabel=None, title=None):
    if xlabel: ax.set_xlabel(xlabel, fontsize=9, labelpad=8)
    if ylabel: ax.set_ylabel(ylabel, fontsize=9, labelpad=8)
    if title:  ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11.5, color=PAL["ink"],
                            loc="left", pad=12, fontweight="semibold")
    return ax

def human(n, _=None):
    """1.4e12 -> '1.4T'. Used for axis ticks and tables alike."""
    n = float(n)
    for div, suf in ((1e12, "T"), (1e9, "B"), (1e6, "M")):
        if abs(n) >= div:
            v = n / div
            return f"{v:.1f}{suf}" if v < 10 else f"{v:.0f}{suf}"
    return f"{n:.0f}"

HUMAN = FuncFormatter(human)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- data
# Hoffmann et al. (2022), Table 1: parameter counts and training tokens as printed.
MODELS = pd.DataFrame([
    ("MT-NLG 530B", 530e9, 270e9,  6*530e9*270e9),
    ("Gopher",      280e9, 300e9,  5.76e23),   # FLOPs as printed, Fig. 2 caption
    ("Jurassic-1",  178e9, 300e9,  6*178e9*300e9),
    ("GPT-3",       175e9, 300e9,  6*175e9*300e9),
    ("LaMDA",       137e9, 168e9,  6*137e9*168e9),
    ("Chinchilla",   70e9, 1.4e12, 5.76e23),
], columns=["model", "params", "tokens", "flops"])
MODELS["tok_per_param"] = MODELS.tokens / MODELS.params

# Porian et al. (2024), Table 1, RefinedWeb column, 95% CIs as printed.
WATERFALL = pd.DataFrame([
    ("Reproducing Kaplan et al.",     0.835, 0.82, 0.85, "Baseline: Kaplan's setup reproduced"),
    ("+ count last-layer FLOPs",      0.706, 0.69, 0.72, "Compute axis now includes the output head"),
    ("+ warmup proportional to $N$",  0.602, 0.59, 0.62, "Replaces a fixed 1.57B-token warmup"),
    ("+ matched cosine decay",        0.571, 0.56, 0.59, "Chinchilla's own proposed explanation"),
    ("+ per-scale optimizer tuning",  0.497, 0.49, 0.50, "LR, batch size and AdamW $\\beta_2$ swept per size"),
], columns=["step", "a", "lo", "hi", "what"])

GOPHER_BUDGET = 5.76e23   # FLOPs, Hoffmann et al. (2022) Fig. 2 caption
```

::: {.callout-important icon=false}
## The short version

1.  **Kaplan et al. (2020)** found that compute-optimal training puts almost
    everything into parameters: $N \propto C^{0.73}$, $D \propto C^{0.27}$.
    Their advice was to train very large models and stop "significantly before
    convergence." [@kaplan2020]

2.  **Hoffmann et al. (2022)**, the Chinchilla paper, found the two should
    scale *equally*: $a \approx b \approx 0.5$, i.e. "for every doubling of model size
    the number of training tokens should also be doubled." A 70B model on 1.4T
    tokens beat the 280B Gopher trained on the same FLOPs. [@hoffmann2022]

3.  **Kaplan's exponent was a methodology artifact**, and it has since been
    reproduced and decomposed. Porian et al. reproduce Kaplan's raw fit (0.835)
    and walk it down to 0.497 by counting the output layer's FLOPs, scaling
    warmup with model size, and tuning the optimizer per scale. Notably, the cosine-schedule explanation
    Chinchilla itself offered accounts for only a small part of the gap. [@porian2024]

4.  **Chinchilla's own Approach 3 is also off.** Epoch AI's replication shows
    its parametric fit disagrees with the paper's other two methods, and that its
    reported confidence intervals would need about 600,000 training runs to be
    that narrow. The cause was an optimizer that stopped before converging.
    [@besiroglu2024] *And* Chinchilla-optimal is the wrong objective if you plan
    to serve the model: it minimizes loss per *training* FLOP and ignores
    inference entirely.
:::

Between 2020 and 2022 almost every frontier lab trained on roughly 300 billion
tokens and competed on parameter count. Given the scaling law they had, that was
the right call: if optimal model size grows like $C^{0.73}$ and optimal token count
like $C^{0.27}$, a 10× compute increase buys 5.4× the parameters and only 1.9× the
data.

Chinchilla showed that the data axis had been starved. Here is what the 2020–2022
generation looked like in tokens per parameter.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ratio
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Training tokens per parameter. Every large model of the Kaplan era sits
#|   between 0.5 and 1.7; Chinchilla sits at 20, on the same training budget as Gopher.
#|   Source: Hoffmann et al. (2022), Table 1. The dashed rule marks ≈20
#|   tokens/parameter, the ratio implied by the paper's Approach 1 projections
#|   (Table 3: a 1B model → 20.2B tokens) and the ratio Chinchilla was trained at.

d = MODELS.sort_values("tok_per_param")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.2))
colors = [PAL["chin"] if m == "Chinchilla" else PAL["kaplan"] for m in d.model]

ax.barh(d.model, d.tok_per_param, height=0.46, color=colors,
        alpha=1.0, zorder=3)
for y, (v, m) in enumerate(zip(d.tok_per_param, d.model)):
    ax.text(v + 0.35, y, f"{v:.2f}", va="center", fontsize=10,
            fontweight="semibold", color=PAL["ink"] if m == "Chinchilla" else PAL["ink2"])

ax.axvline(20, color=PAL["chin"], lw=1.4, ls=(0, (4, 3)), alpha=.7, zorder=2)
ax.text(20, len(d) - 0.35, "Chinchilla-optimal ≈ 20  ", ha="right", va="bottom",
        fontsize=9.5, color=PAL["chin"], fontweight="semibold")

ax.set_xlim(0, 23)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0, labelcolor=PAL["ink"], labelsize=10.5)
style(ax, xlabel="TRAINING TOKENS PER PARAMETER")
plt.show()
```

## What each paper actually fit

The two papers are not two measurements of the same quantity. They fit different
equations to different data, and the difference in form matters as much as the
difference in exponent.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
**Kaplan et al. 2020**, Eq. 1.1–1.3

$$
L(N) = \left(\tfrac{N_c}{N}\right)^{\alpha_N}\!,\quad
L(D) = \left(\tfrac{D_c}{D}\right)^{\alpha_D}\!,\quad
L(C_{\min}) = \left(\tfrac{C_c}{C_{\min}}\right)^{\alpha_C}
$$

$\alpha_N = 0.076,\ N_c = 8.8\!\times\!10^{13}$
$\alpha_D = 0.095,\ D_c = 5.4\!\times\!10^{13}$
$\alpha_C^{\min} = 0.050,\ C_c^{\min} = 3.1\!\times\!10^{8}$ PF-days

*Pure power laws, no offset.* Loss goes to zero as $N \to \infty$. $N$ counts
**non-embedding** parameters, "excluding all vocabulary and positional
embeddings." Models spanned 768 to 1.5B non-embedding params; data 22M to 23B
tokens.

**Hoffmann et al. 2022**, Eq. 2 / Eq. 10

$$
L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}}
$$

$E = 1.6934,\ A = 406.4,\ B = 410.7$
$\alpha = 0.3392,\ \beta = 0.2849$ (TeX-source precision)
$a = \beta/(\alpha{+}\beta) = 0.46$

*An irreducible-loss term.* $E$ is the entropy of natural text you can never fit
away. $N$ is **total** parameters, embeddings included. Models ran up to 16B
params, budgets $6\!\times\!10^{18} \to 3\!\times\!10^{21}$ FLOPs.
:::

Three structural differences matter here. Kaplan's form has no offset $E$, so the
fit has to bend its exponents to absorb the flattening it sees at scale. Kaplan
excludes embedding parameters and Chinchilla includes them; at 768 non-embedding
parameters with a 50,257-token vocabulary, the embedding matrix is effectively the
whole model. And both use $C \approx 6ND$, but Kaplan's $N$ leaves out the output
layer, an under-count Porian et al. put at "roughly 10% at larger models to roughly
90% at smaller models."

Put the two allocation rules on the same axes and the practical consequence is
immediate.

```{python}
#| label: laws
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The two allocation laws, as published"

def kaplan_N(C):
    """Kaplan Fig. 14 / Table 6: N = 1.3e9 * (C_min / 1 PF-day)^0.73, non-embedding
    params. 'Adjusted' for batch size, as Porian et al. (2024) call it."""
    return 1.3e9 * (C / 8.64e19) ** 0.73

def chinchilla_N(C):
    """Chinchilla Approach 1, anchored on Hoffmann et al. Table 3
    (67B parameters at the 5.76e23 FLOP Gopher budget)."""
    return 6.7e10 * (C / GOPHER_BUDGET) ** 0.50
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-frontier
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Compute-optimal model size under each law, extrapolated across the budgets
#|   labs actually spent. Model markers use each paper's published parameter and
#|   token counts; compute for GPT-3, Jurassic-1, LaMDA and MT-NLG is 6ND (our
#|   arithmetic), while Gopher and Chinchilla use the 5.76e23 FLOPs printed in
#|   Hoffmann et al. Fig. 2. Kaplan's curve is in non-embedding parameters, so
#|   the gap to Chinchilla is slightly overstated at small budgets.

C = np.logspace(19, 26, 300)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5.2))

ax.plot(C, kaplan_N(C), color=PAL["kaplan"], lw=2.2, zorder=4)
ax.plot(C, chinchilla_N(C), color=PAL["chin"], lw=2.2, zorder=4)

ax.annotate(r"Kaplan  $N \propto C^{0.73}$", (3e22, kaplan_N(3e22)),
            xytext=(-8, 10), textcoords="offset points", ha="right",
            color=PAL["kaplan"], fontsize=11, fontweight="semibold")
ax.annotate(r"Chinchilla  $N \propto C^{0.50}$", (1.3e24, chinchilla_N(1.3e24)),
            xytext=(8, -20), textcoords="offset points", ha="left",
            color=PAL["chin"], fontsize=11, fontweight="semibold")

# the divergence at the Gopher budget
gk, gc = kaplan_N(GOPHER_BUDGET), chinchilla_N(GOPHER_BUDGET)
ax.plot([GOPHER_BUDGET] * 2, [gc, gk], color=PAL["ink2"], lw=1, ls=(0, (2, 2)), zorder=3)
ax.annotate(f"Kaplan would build {human(gk)} here, {gk/gc:.0f}× Chinchilla",
            (GOPHER_BUDGET, gk), xytext=(-10, 8), textcoords="offset points",
            ha="right", fontsize=9.5, color=PAL["ink2"], fontweight="semibold")

OFF = {"MT-NLG 530B": (11, 0, "left"), "Gopher": (11, 0, "left"),
       "Jurassic-1": (-7, 9, "right"), "GPT-3": (0, -15, "center"),
       "LaMDA": (-11, 0, "right"), "Chinchilla": (0, -16, "center")}
for r in MODELS.itertuples():
    c = PAL["chin"] if r.model == "Chinchilla" else PAL["ink2"]
    ax.scatter(r.flops, r.params, s=48, color=c, zorder=6,
               edgecolor=PAL["surface"], linewidth=2)
    dx, dy, ha = OFF[r.model]
    ax.annotate(r.model, (r.flops, r.params), xytext=(dx, dy),
                textcoords="offset points", ha=ha, va="center",
                fontsize=9.5, color=c, fontweight="semibold", zorder=7)

ax.set(xscale="log", yscale="log", xlim=(1e19, 1e26), ylim=(1e8, 3e12))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(HUMAN)
style(ax, xlabel="TRAINING COMPUTE $C$ (FLOPs)",
      ylabel="COMPUTE-OPTIMAL PARAMETERS $N^*$")
plt.show()
```

## Three approaches, and one that doesn't agree

Chinchilla's credibility rests on measuring the same quantity three independent
ways. Two agree tightly. The third, the one everybody quotes because it gives
you a closed-form equation, is the odd one out.

| Approach | $a$ ($N^* \propto C^a$) | interval | $b$ ($D^* \propto C^b$) | interval |
|:---|---:|:---:|---:|:---:|
| 1. Minimum over training curves | 0.50 | (0.488, 0.502) | 0.50 | (0.501, 0.512) |
| 2. IsoFLOP profiles | 0.49 | (0.462, 0.534) | 0.51 | (0.483, 0.529) |
| 3. Parametric loss modelling | 0.46 | (0.454, 0.455) | 0.54 | (0.542, 0.543) |
| Kaplan et al. (2020) | 0.73 | — | 0.27 | — |

: Hoffmann et al. (2022), Table 2. 10th/90th percentiles from bootstrap. {#tbl-approaches tbl-colwidths="[40,12,18,12,18]"}

**Approach 1** takes the minimum over training curves: train a fixed set of model
sizes, vary the token count, and read off the envelope. **Approach 2** runs IsoFLOP
profiles: nine fixed FLOP budgets from $6\times10^{18}$ to $3\times10^{21}$,
sweeping model size within each and finding the parabola's minimum. **Approach 3**
fits the parametric loss and derives the frontier analytically.

Approach 3's $a = 0.46$ looks close enough to 0.5 to ignore. It is not, for two
reasons: the fitted constants already put the ratio near 40 tokens per parameter
at $10^{22}$ FLOPs, and the 0.08 gap between $b$ and $a$ makes it climb from
there. You can check both from the paper's own printed constants.

```{python}
#| label: repro-a3

# Hoffmann et al. (2022), Eq. 10 constants. Printed as 0.34 / 0.28 in the body;
# the extra digits come from the arXiv TeX source, recovered by Besiroglu et al.
HOFFMANN = dict(E=1.6934, A=406.4,  B=410.7,   alpha=0.3392, beta=0.2849)
EPOCH    = dict(E=1.8172, A=482.01, B=2085.43, alpha=0.3478, beta=0.3658)

def loss(N, D, E, A, B, alpha, beta):
    """Predicted cross-entropy for N parameters trained on D tokens."""
    return E + A / N**alpha + B / D**beta

def frontier(C, E, A, B, alpha, beta):
    """Closed-form compute-optimal (N*, D*) for budget C. Hoffmann Eq. 4."""
    a = beta / (alpha + beta)
    b = alpha / (alpha + beta)
    G = (alpha * A / (beta * B)) ** (1 / (alpha + beta))
    return G * (C / 6) ** a, (C / 6) ** b / G

N_star, D_star = frontier(GOPHER_BUDGET, **HOFFMANN)
print(f"N* = {N_star/1e9:.1f}B   D* = {D_star/1e12:.2f}T   D/N = {D_star/N_star:.0f}")
```

That 40.3B is a genuine check on the arithmetic: Hoffmann et al.'s Figure 4
caption reads *"We project the optimal model size given the Gopher FLOP budget to
be 40B parameters."* The constants reproduce the paper's own figure.

But look at the ratio the same code prints. Approach 3 says **59 tokens per
parameter** at the Gopher budget, and the number keeps climbing with compute.
Approach 1, on the same budget, says 67B parameters on 1.5T tokens: **22 tokens
per parameter**. The paper trained Chinchilla at 20. Its own headline model does
not follow its own headline equation.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## The replication

Besiroglu et al. digitised 240 points from Hoffmann's Figure 4 (they converted the
figure to SVG and mapped each point's fill colour back to a loss value) and refit
the law. Their result is
$L(N,D) = 1.8172 + 482.01\,N^{-0.3478} + 2085.43\,D^{-0.3658}$, giving
$a = 0.5126$ (SE 0.02). That agrees with Approaches 1 and 2, and with how
Chinchilla was actually trained. They also note the published intervals on $a$
(0.454–0.455) are implausibly tight: *"intervals this narrow would require over
600,000 experiments, while they likely only ran fewer than 500."* [@besiroglu2024]

The cause, confirmed by one of Hoffmann's lead authors: the Huber loss was
averaged rather than summed over points, so L-BFGS hit its stopping tolerance
early, both in the main fit and in every bootstrap.
:::

Swap the Epoch constants into the same function and the ratio stabilises where
practitioners expect it:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Compute-optimal allocation under Hoffmann's Approach 3 versus Epoch AI's refit."

rows = []
for C_budget in [1e22, 1e23, GOPHER_BUDGET, 1e25]:
    nh, dh = frontier(C_budget, **HOFFMANN)
    ne, de = frontier(C_budget, **EPOCH)
    rows.append({
        "Compute (FLOPs)":  f"{C_budget:.1e}",
        "Hoffmann A3 N*": human(nh), "Hoffmann A3 tok/param": f"{dh/nh:.0f}",
        "Epoch N*":       human(ne), "Epoch tok/param":       f"{de/ne:.0f}",
    })
pd.DataFrame(rows)
```

The Epoch refit stays between 17 and 20 tokens per parameter across three orders
of magnitude, drifting slowly down rather than up. That stability is what makes "20 tokens per parameter" a usable rule of thumb rather than a
coincidence at one budget. Note that the rule comes from Approaches 1 and 2 and
the replication, *not* from the equation most people copy.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isoflop
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >
#|   IsoFLOP curves drawn straight from Hoffmann et al.'s published loss function,
#|   with tokens set by D = C/6N. No refitting. At the Gopher budget the minimum
#|   lands at about 40B, matching the paper's stated 40B projection. These are the
#|   model's predictions, not measured runs. The paper's *measured* IsoFLOP
#|   minima (Approach 2) sit closer to 63B at that budget.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.8))
N = np.logspace(8.4, 12, 400)

for C_budget, col in [(1e21, PAL["third"]), (1e23, PAL["kaplan"]),
                      (GOPHER_BUDGET, PAL["chin"])]:
    D = C_budget / (6 * N)
    L = loss(N, D, **HOFFMANN)
    ax.plot(N, L, color=col, lw=2.2, zorder=4,
            label=f"C = {C_budget:.1e} FLOPs")
    i = int(np.argmin(L))
    ax.scatter(N[i], L[i], s=48, color=col, zorder=6,
               edgecolor=PAL["surface"], linewidth=2)
    ax.vlines(N[i], L[i], 1.85, color=col, lw=1, ls=(0, (2, 2)), alpha=.55, zorder=3)
    ax.annotate(human(N[i]), (N[i], L[i]), xytext=(0, 11),
                textcoords="offset points", ha="center",
                fontsize=10, color=col, fontweight="semibold")

ax.set(xscale="log", xlim=(3e8, 1e12), ylim=(1.85, 2.75))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(HUMAN)
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=9.5, labelcolor=PAL["ink2"])
style(ax, xlabel="MODEL PARAMETERS $N$", ylabel="PREDICTED LOSS (NATS)")
plt.show()
```

## Where 0.73 actually came from

Chinchilla's own explanation for the discrepancy was the learning-rate schedule:
Kaplan used one cosine decay sized for about 131B tokens across all runs, so a model
evaluated at an intermediate checkpoint looks worse than a model whose schedule
was sized to stop there. That makes short runs look worse than they are, and pushes
the fit toward bigger models on less data.

It is a good hypothesis. It is also mostly wrong, and we know this because Porian
et al. ran over 900 training runs (16 model sizes from 5M to 901M parameters on
OpenWebText2 and RefinedWeb), reproducing Kaplan's setup and then removing one
confounder at a time.

One wrinkle before the numbers. Kaplan's raw fit was actually $N \propto C^{0.88}$;
the famous 0.73 is their *adjusted* law, after correcting for using too large a
batch at small scale. Porian et al.'s baseline (0.835 on RefinedWeb) reproduces
the raw 0.88 setup, and their per-scale tuning step does roughly the job Kaplan's
batch adjustment did. They check this directly: with tuned hyperparameters but the
head-FLOP and warmup issues put back, they get 0.717, essentially Kaplan's 0.73
(their Appendix H). So the gap from 0.73 to 0.5 is mostly the two fixes below.

```{python}
#| label: fig-waterfall
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Walking Kaplan's exponent to Chinchilla's, one fix at a time. Each point is a
#|   re-measurement of *a* after one more correction; the last step also switches
#|   to a constant learning rate. Source: Porian et al. (2024), Table 1, RefinedWeb column, with
#|   95% confidence intervals as printed. Their OpenWebText2 column follows the
#|   same path (0.864 → 0.699 → 0.603 → 0.574 → 0.518).

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.6))
ys = np.arange(len(WATERFALL))[::-1]

for y, r in zip(ys, WATERFALL.itertuples()):
    col = PAL["chin"] if r.Index == len(WATERFALL) - 1 else PAL["kaplan"]
    if r.Index > 0:
        prev = WATERFALL.a[r.Index - 1]
        ax.barh(y, prev - r.a, left=r.a, height=0.20, color=col, alpha=.22, zorder=2)
        ax.plot([prev, prev], [y, y + 1], color=PAL["rule_strong"],
                lw=0.9, ls=(0, (2, 3)), zorder=2)
        ax.annotate(f"{r.a - prev:+.3f}", ((prev + r.a) / 2, y + 0.22), ha="center",
                    fontsize=9, color=col, fontweight="semibold")
    ax.hlines(y, r.lo, r.hi, color=col, lw=2, zorder=4)
    ax.scatter(r.a, y, s=54, color=col, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(f"{r.a:.3f}", (0.905, y), ha="left", va="center",
                fontsize=10.5, color=PAL["ink"], fontweight="semibold")

ax.axvline(0.5, color=PAL["chin"], lw=1.4, ls=(0, (4, 3)), alpha=.75, zorder=3)
ax.annotate("Chinchilla 0.50", (0.5, len(WATERFALL) - 0.45), ha="center",
            va="bottom", fontsize=9.5, color=PAL["chin"], fontweight="semibold")

ax.set_yticks(ys, [f"{s}\n{w}" for s, w in zip(WATERFALL.step, WATERFALL.what)])
ax.set(xlim=(0.4, 0.93), ylim=(-0.75, len(WATERFALL) - 0.15))
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0, labelcolor=PAL["ink"], labelsize=9.5)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
style(ax, xlabel="FITTED EXPONENT $a$  IN  $N^* \\propto C^{a}$")
plt.show()
```

### 1. Count the output layer's FLOPs (−0.13)

Kaplan excluded embeddings from $N$ and, probably because the output head shared
weights with the input embedding, its per-token FLOPs were left out of the compute
count too. The resulting
under-approximation of compute runs from "roughly 10% at larger models to roughly
90% at smaller models," a bias that scales with the very axis you are fitting
against. Counting it correctly moves $a$ from 0.835 to 0.706.

Pearce & Song come at a closely related issue analytically: model total parameters as $N_T = N_E + \omega N_E^{1/3}$ (fitting
$\omega = 47{,}491$ to Chinchilla's own configurations) and the non-embedding
relationship stops being a power law at all. It has a small-scale regime, a
large-scale regime and a transition between them, with the crossover where
embeddings are half the model, around $10^7$ non-embedding parameters. Kaplan's entire sweep, 768 to 1.5B,
straddles that. Taking the Chinchilla (or Epoch) loss surface and measuring it in Kaplan's
non-embedding units, they get a local exponent of 0.74 (or 0.78). Their
decomposition puts more weight on the embedding convention than Porian's does,
partly because a fitted loss surface has no warmup problem to find. [@pearce2024]

### 2. Stop warming up for 1.57B tokens (−0.10)

This is the subtle one. Kaplan used a fixed 3,000-step warmup at a $2^{19}$-token
batch, about **1.57 billion warmup tokens**, identical for every model. For a
small model at a small budget, the compute-optimal token count is *at or below the
warmup length*. Those runs never leave warmup, so they look terrible, so small
models look worse than they are, so the fit tilts toward large models. Setting
warmup tokens proportional to $N$ moves $a$ to 0.602.

### 3. Tune the optimizer per scale (−0.07)

Sweeping learning rate, batch size and AdamW's $\beta_2$ per model size lands at
**$a = 0.497$, 95% CI (0.49, 0.50)**. Along the way they fit
$\mathrm{BS} = 0.00037\,N^{0.703}$ and $\mathrm{LR} = 3.7\,N^{-0.36}$, and find
the usual $\beta_2 = 0.95$ is too low at small batch sizes. This last step also
switches to a constant learning rate. Their summary: the exponent matches 0.5 "to
within 0.6%" and the predicted model size at Chinchilla compute lands "within 15%
of Chinchilla's size."

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## And the cosine schedule?

Porian et al. tested it in isolation (§3.4) and it moves $a$ from 0.60 to 0.57, and
"most of the gap remains." Their reasoning: with decay targeted at about 131B
tokens, Kaplan's compute-constrained runs "see virtually no learning rate decay,"
less than 1.5% of the decay. Their final 0.497 is achieved with a *constant* learning
rate. Pearce & Song find the same thing independently: switching from Kaplan's
schedule to Chinchilla's *raised* their coefficient from 0.46 to 0.49 rather than
lowering it.
:::

So the field's canonical story, that Kaplan got it wrong because of the
learning-rate schedule, is itself wrong. The dominant factors are an accounting error in the
compute axis and a warmup length that poisoned the small-model end of the fit.

## What each law tells you to build

Four laws, one budget.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-planner
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the allocation code"
#| tbl-cap: "Each row applies one published law to the same training budget. Kaplan uses the adjusted law with D = C/6N; Chinchilla A1 uses the Table 3 anchor; A3 and the Epoch refit use the closed form. Extrapolating any of these far beyond its fitting range is exactly the move this whole story is a cautionary tale about."

def allocate(C):
    kN = kaplan_N(C);     kD = C / (6 * kN)
    cN = chinchilla_N(C); cD = C / (6 * cN)
    hN, hD = frontier(C, **HOFFMANN)
    eN, eD = frontier(C, **EPOCH)
    return [("Kaplan 2020 (adjusted)", kN, kD),
            ("Chinchilla · Approach 1", cN, cD),
            ("Chinchilla · Approach 3", hN, hD),
            ("Epoch AI refit (2024)",   eN, eD)]

BUDGETS = {"Chinchilla / Gopher": GOPHER_BUDGET, "1e24": 1e24, "Llama 3 405B": 3.8e25}

def ratio(r):
    return f"{r:.2f}" if r < 1 else (f"{r:.1f}" if r < 10 else f"{r:,.0f}")

out = []
for name, C_budget in BUDGETS.items():
    for law, n, d in allocate(C_budget):
        out.append({"Budget": name, "Law": law, "N*": human(n),
                    "D*": human(d), "tok/param": ratio(d / n)})
pd.DataFrame(out).set_index(["Budget", "Law"])
```

## Chinchilla-optimal is not deployment-optimal

Here is the part that matters most for anyone shipping a model, and it is a
limitation both papers share rather than a disagreement between them. Both
optimise *loss given a training budget*. Neither includes a single inference FLOP.
If you train once and serve billions of tokens, you are optimising the wrong
objective.

### Add inference to the objective

Sardana et al. invert the problem: fix a quality target, minimise total compute.
Training costs $6N$ per token, inference costs $2N$ per token, so the objective
becomes [@sardana2024]

$$
N^*,\, D^*_{\text{tr}} \;=\;
\operatorname*{argmin}_{N,\, D_{\text{tr}} \;\mid\; L(N, D_{\text{tr}}) = \ell}
\;\; 6N D_{\text{tr}} + 2N D_{\text{inf}}
$$

where $D_{\text{inf}}$ is total lifetime inference tokens, input plus output. With
$D_{\text{inf}} > 0$ there is no closed form; they solve it by root-finding. It is
short enough to reproduce:

```{python}
#| label: inference-aware

from scipy.optimize import brentq, minimize_scalar

# Sardana et al. Appendix A: Chinchilla's A, B, E with alpha = 0.336, beta = 0.283,
# taken from De Vries (2023) to better match Hoffmann's Table A3 (not the
# TeX-source values above).
SARDANA = dict(E=1.69, A=406.4, B=410.7, alpha=0.336, beta=0.283)

def tokens_for_loss(N, target, E, A, B, alpha, beta):
    """Tokens needed for N parameters to reach a given loss."""
    residual = target - E - A / N**alpha
    return np.inf if residual <= 0 else (B / residual) ** (1 / beta)

def total_flops(N, target, D_inf, p):
    return 6 * N * tokens_for_loss(N, target, **p) + 2 * N * D_inf

def inference_aware(N_chinchilla, D_inf, p=SARDANA):
    """Cheapest (N, D) reaching the quality of a Chinchilla-optimal model
    of size N_chinchilla, once D_inf inference tokens are paid for."""
    budget = 10 ** brentq(lambda lc: frontier(10**lc, **p)[0] - N_chinchilla, 18, 30)
    N0, D0 = frontier(budget, **p)
    target = loss(N0, D0, **p)
    floor = (p["A"] / (target - p["E"])) ** (1 / p["alpha"])   # N below this can't reach it
    best = minimize_scalar(lambda x: total_flops(np.exp(x), target, D_inf, p),
                           bounds=(np.log(floor * 1.001), np.log(N_chinchilla)),
                           method="bounded")
    N1 = np.exp(best.x)
    saved = 1 - total_flops(N1, target, D_inf, p) / total_flops(N0, target, D_inf, p)
    return N0, D0, N1, tokens_for_loss(N1, target, **p), saved

N0, D0, N1, D1, saved = inference_aware(30e9, D_inf=1e13)
print(f"Chinchilla-optimal : {N0/1e9:5.1f}B on {D0/1e12:.2f}T tokens")
print(f"Inference-aware    : {N1/1e9:5.1f}B on {D1/1e12:.2f}T tokens "
      f"({D1/D0:.2f}x the data)")
print(f"Total FLOPs saved  : {saved:.0%}")
```

That reproduces the paper's stated result exactly: a developer expecting a
30B-Chinchilla-quality model to see $10^{13}$ inference tokens "can reduce their
total FLOPs by 28% by training a 13.6B model on 2.84× the data." In dollar terms,
with realistic MFU asymmetry between training and autoregressive generation, the
same quality target at 17.5B requests is reached ~58% cheaper by an 8.58B model
trained on 12.1T tokens.

::: {.callout-caution icon=false}
## The caveat, from the same paper

Fitting scaling-law coefficients only on typical token/parameter ratios
"overestimates the impact of additional tokens at these extreme ranges."
Refitting with their extreme-ratio data (47 models, 150M–6B, up to 10,000
tokens/param) gives $\alpha = 0.18$, $\beta = 0.24$ against Chinchilla's
0.34 / 0.28. Extrapolating Chinchilla's constants out to 1,000+ tokens/param
will flatter your plan.
:::

### What if you run out of data?

Muennighoff et al. ran more than 400 models, 10M to 9B parameters, for up to 1,500
epochs, and their finding is unusually actionable: **up to roughly 4 epochs of
repeated data is nearly free**. Their 8.7B model at four epochs on 44B unique
tokens ended "with only 0.5% higher validation loss than the single-epoch model."
Returns then decay fast, with $R_D^* \approx 15$ repetitions as the point where repeated tokens have
lost about 63% of their value, and runs at 44 epochs diverge outright. They model it by replacing
$D$ with effective data [@muennighoff2023]

$$
D' = U_D + U_D \, R_D^* \left(1 - e^{-R_D / R_D^*}\right)
$$

which collapses to Chinchilla exactly when there is no repetition. Under data
constraint they also find you should scale epochs faster than parameters, the
opposite tilt to Chinchilla's equal scaling.

### What frontier labs actually did

The folk version is that Meta over-trained Llama 3. Only partly. Meta's Llama 3
paper reports IsoFLOPs experiments from $6\times10^{18}$ to $10^{22}$ FLOPs,
extrapolating to a $3.8\times10^{25}$ FLOP budget and suggesting "training a 402B
parameter model on 16.55T tokens." They trained 405B on 15.6T, *approximately
compute-optimal*, not over-trained. The over-training was deliberate and confined
to the small models: "we also train our smaller models for much longer than is
compute-optimal… The resulting models perform better than compute-optimal models
at the same inference budget." [@llama3]

Note the ratio: 15.6T tokens on 405B parameters is about 39 tokens per parameter,
and Meta's own fit (402B on 16.55T) says 41. That is roughly double Chinchilla's
20, from IsoFLOP curves on their own data mix. The planner table above, which puts
Chinchilla-optimal at 544B on 12T for the same budget, shows how much the
"optimal" ratio moves with the data and stack.

That is how Meta split the problem, and it is how I would split it. Chinchilla-optimal is the right target for
the flagship, where training cost dominates; heavy over-training is the right
target for the models you actually serve.

## The practitioner's checklist

-   Never use Kaplan's allocation exponents. 0.73/0.27 is a measurement
    artifact with a known, reproduced cause. The loss-vs-scale *phenomenology*
    (smooth power laws, predictable returns) survives intact.
-   Use ~20 tokens/parameter as a starting anchor, not a constant. It comes
    from Approaches 1 and 2 plus the Epoch refit, not from Chinchilla's published
    Eq. 10, which drifts to 59+ at frontier budgets. Meta's own IsoFLOP fit for
    Llama 3 landed near 40.
-   If you will serve the model, over-train it. Compute the inference-inclusive
    objective before sizing. At $10^{12}$–$10^{13}$ lifetime tokens the optimum
    moves substantially smaller-and-longer.
-   Fit your own law on your own data and stack. Every exponent here is
    entangled with tokenizer, data mix, optimizer tuning and architecture.
    Chinchilla's own three approaches disagreed on their own data.
-   Sweep hyperparameters per scale, and warm up proportionally to model size.
    Kaplan's discrepancy traces back to holding warmup and optimizer settings fixed
    across scales that should not have been.
-   Check that your scaling-law fit actually converged. Chinchilla's Approach 3
    constants came from an L-BFGS run that stopped early because the Huber loss was
    averaged instead of summed, which is also why its bootstrap intervals came out
    absurdly narrow.
-   Include the output layer in your FLOP accounting. The single largest term
    in the reconciliation was an accounting choice.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## The meta-lesson

Kaplan's paper was careful, influential, and wrong about one thing, and the field
spent two years and a lot of compute acting on it. Chinchilla corrected it, and had
a serious flaw of its own in the very equation everyone copied. Both were caught
only when independent groups re-derived the numbers from scratch, which is a good
argument for re-fitting before you trust anyone's constants, including the ones in
this note.
:::
